results.name: shared_final_digit_match_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets that end in the final digit shared by all (>=2) examples (e.g. 28,98 -> 38, 58); observed > null means the model under-endorses targets fitting a shared last-digit rule (treats it as just one diluted property), observed < null means it over-endorses them.

results.name: size_principle_violator_gap
results.description: Among parity-homogeneous sets, yes-rate for parity-VIOLATING targets in 3-4-example sets minus in 2-example sets; observed < null means people reject rule violators more sharply as examples accumulate (a size-principle effect the model lacks), observed > null the reverse.

results.name: parity_only_hit_dilution_slope
results.description: For parity-homogeneous sets, among targets that match the shared parity but none of the set's other shared multiple-of-m (3..12) or final-digit properties, the yes-rate in sets with >=2 such extra shared properties minus sets with 0; the model's normalized overlap predicts strong dilution (negative), so observed > null means people treat parity as sufficient regardless of how many other properties the examples share, observed < null means dilution is even stronger.

results.name: odd_set_even_target_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for even targets when all (>=2) examples are odd; observed > null means the model's single parity salience makes people look stricter about odd sets than they are (people tolerate parity violations of odd sets), observed < null the reverse.

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets numerically closer to the last-shown example than the first minus targets closer to the first; the model ignores example order, so observed > null means a recency effect (the latest example anchors generalization), observed < null a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: In multi-example sets, yes-rate for targets numerically closer to the last-shown example than the first minus targets closer to the first; the model ignores example order, so observed > null means a recency effect (the latest example anchors generalization), observed < null a primacy effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    f, l = {}, {}
    for s in sets.unique():
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        f[s], l[s] = ex[0], ex[-1]
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    df_ = np.abs(t - sets.map(f).to_numpy())
    dl = np.abs(t - sets.map(l).to_numpy())
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    multi = (sets.str.count(",") >= 1).to_numpy()
    a = multi & (dl < df_)
    b = multi & (df_ < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: round_number_target_bonus
results.description: In sets whose examples are not all multiples of 10, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of 10 minus other targets of the same parity as the set (even sets only); observed > null means people favour round-number targets a priori (a bias the model, which only credits shared properties, lacks), observed < null the reverse.

results.name: unstructured_set_inside_span_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets strictly inside [min,max] of sets whose examples do NOT share parity; observed < null means the model over-endorses in-span targets when there is no shared arithmetic rule (its magnitude bounds dominate a near-empty profile), observed > null means people generalize across the span even more than predicted.

results.name: even_set_multiple_of_four_advantage
results.description: In all-even sets whose examples are all multiples of 4, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of 4 minus even targets that are not; the model ties x4 to the same 'multiples' salience as x3/x9, so observed < null means it over-credits the x4 rule in even sets (people just use evenness), observed > null means it under-credits it.
